items.title: Tanker becomes the battlefield: US and Iran now trade ship-for-ship strikes
items.idea: US CENTCOM disabled or destroyed 3 Iranian crude carriers Saturday (M/T Downy near Kharg Island, M/T Stark 1 near Jask, M/T Kylo/Noxen destroyed in the Gulf of Oman) after Iranian missiles targeted US Navy vessels. Iran claims retaliatory strikes on 3 tankers plus 3 US-linked vessels. Before the war, roughly 90% of Iran's crude exports moved through Kharg — the terminal itself hasn't been struck yet, and that's the real tail risk left on the table.
items.angle: This is the oil supply risk that a VIX sitting near multi-month lows is completely mispricing — 'tanker for tanker' makes escalation structural into Monday's open, not incidental.
items.tweetA: US Navy dodges Iranian missiles, then destroys 3 Iranian oil tankers in response. That's not de-escalation, that's a standing 'tanker for tanker' doctrine now in its 2nd week. Watch war-risk insurance premiums once insurers realize the exchange rate isn't fixed. $USO $BNO
items.tweetB: 90% of Iran's crude used to move through one island, Kharg. The US hasn't hit the terminal, only ships near it. That's the whole ballgame: Washington is testing how much pressure it can apply without triggering the response nobody wants. VIX at cycle lows says nobody's pricing that test failing.

items.title: The retaliation formula IS the escalation: commercial ships to warships in 4 days
items.idea: Sept 1 tanker strikes were retaliation for attacks on commercial shipping. By Sept 5 the same 'tanker for tanker' rule applied after an attack on US warships that caused zero casualties — the covered offense expanded in under a week while the punishment class stayed identical. Five Iranian government-linked tankers have now reportedly been struck under the rule, with the latest hit near Kharg's loading terminal (not the terminal itself).
items.angle: A game-theory read on the same story as item 1 — treats it as a policy-design problem (a 'widening license,' not a fixed tariff), which is the sharper way to underwrite how fast this spirals.
items.tweetA: Sept 1: US hits 2 Iranian tankers for an attack on commercial shipping. Sept 5: US hits 3 more for an attack that hurt zero Americans. Same punishment, expanding crime list. That's not deterrence, that's a ratchet with no defined stopping point.
items.tweetB: Everyone's asking if Hormuz closes. Wrong question. The right one: is 'tanker for tanker' a bounded tariff or an open-ended license? A tariff needs a fixed exchange rate. This one's price has already gone up twice in a week.

items.title: VIX at Trump-term lows, 30Y at generational highs — pricing two different worlds
items.idea: Global bond yields sit at generational highs while the VIX trades near the lowest levels of Trump's second term and the MSCI World is within 1% of its record. Equity multiples have compressed even as the index held up, and momentum has surrendered roughly half its summer gains. Goldman flags geopolitical energy risk and AI-capex competition for capital as the two main right-tail threats to rates — but suspects the market may already be overpricing both.
items.angle: The VIX/30Y divergence is the same complacency showing up twice — once in vol, once in the tanker headlines nobody's hedging (items 1-2). Pair with the Eliant Fear-Greed chart (item 6) for a breadth-vs-headline-risk story.
items.tweetA: 30-year yields at generational highs. VIX at the lowest of Trump's second term. Someone is wrong. Either equity vol catches up to what bonds are pricing, or bonds are wrong about inflation persistence. I know which side I'd rather not be short.
items.tweetB: Goldman says AI capex competing for capital and Middle East oil risk are the two things that break the long end higher — then says the market might already be overpricing both. Translation: they don't know either. That's the actual signal.

items.title: Gulf oil exports already back to 15-16mbpd — the inflation risk moved to diesel, not crude
items.idea: Goldman estimates Persian Gulf oil exports have recovered to roughly 15 to 16 million barrels per day despite the conflict, meaning the crude supply scare has largely resolved. The real inflation risk has rotated into refined products: European natural gas near its highs, diesel markets 'considerably more stressed' — the molecules factories, trucks and households actually burn. Fed vote count: Kevin Warsh hawkish, Waller giving room to hold unless this week's CPI/PPI run hot. Goldman still favors higher DM long-end yields, curve steepeners, and is short European long-end rates.
items.angle: Directly contradicts the tanker-headline panic in items 1-2 — Goldman's own barrel-count says crude supply is fine, so further oil pain from here is a shipping/insurance problem, not production, and it shows up in diesel before it shows up in Brent.
items.tweetA: Goldman: Gulf oil exports already back to 15-16mbpd. Crude supply crisis? Basically over. The actual inflation risk snuck into diesel and European nat gas while everyone watched Brent. Factories and truckers feel that before CPI does.
items.tweetB: Fed vote count into CPI week: Warsh hawkish, Waller dovish-leaning unless the print is hot. Goldman's trade isn't 'will the Fed hike' — it's curve steepeners and short European long-end rates regardless of the answer. That's the more interesting read.

items.title: Washington is quietly testing whether Russia will trade Iran for a Ukraine deal
items.idea: Days before Witkoff and Kushner's 3-hour Moscow meeting with Putin, CIA Director Ratcliffe made his own Moscow trip and reportedly pressed Russia to reduce economic and military support for Iran. Russia and Iran signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in January 2025 covering defense, nuclear tech and de-dollarized banking, plus joint investment in the International North-South Transport Corridor through Iran. Putin ordered no Kyiv strikes for 3 days and Zelensky reciprocated on Moscow — a narrow diplomatic corridor, not a ceasefire.
items.angle: The market treats Ukraine and Iran as separate books; Washington is explicitly trying to trade leverage between them. Any wobble in Russia's Iran calculus is a bigger geopolitical shift than the Hormuz headlines alone.
items.tweetA: Ratcliffe goes to Moscow, presses Russia on Iran. Days later Witkoff and Kushner sit with Putin for 3 hours on Ukraine. Nobody's calling this a linked negotiation officially. It obviously is. Watch Russia-Iran, not just Russia-Ukraine, for the next tell.
items.tweetB: Putin doesn't need to drop Iran to move this market — he just needs to look like he might. A 20-year strategic treaty isn't worth much if the other party starts wondering whether Moscow would trade it away for a Washington deal. That uncertainty alone is pressure on Tehran.

items.title: S&P is 120bps from all-time highs and the Fear-Greed index is back in 'fear'
items.idea: The 10Y briefly touched 4.8% intraweek before that level acted as a hard ceiling, aided by dovish Waller comments; indices closed nearly flat (Qs +30bps best, Dow -20bps worst). Breadth has reset without a real price drawdown: only 45% of stocks sit above their 20-day average and roughly 50% above their 50-day — both neutral, not oversold — yet the Fear-Greed index has swung back to 'fear' while the S&P sits just 120bps off record highs. CPI/PPI this week are framed as the deciding factor for a 'practically 50-50' September Fed decision.
items.angle: A market that's basically flat and near highs shouldn't have 'fear' positioning — that gap between price and sentiment is exactly the kind of quiet setup that resolves violently once CPI prints either way this week.
items.tweetA: S&P is 120bps off all-time highs. The Fear-Greed index just rotated into 'fear' anyway. Price hasn't cracked, but positioning already has. High but scared is usually a coiled spring, and CPI this week is the trigger.
items.tweetB: 50-50 odds on a September hike, per the street. That's not a market that's priced anything — it's a market refusing to commit. Whichever way CPI breaks this week resolves both the Fed call and the fear-vs-price gap at once. $SPY $QQQ

items.title: MAGA Inc drops $10M on ads for Paxton's Senate bid — a proxy fight over a year early
items.idea: FEC filings show MAGA Inc, Trump's main Super PAC, directed $10 million toward attack ads supporting Texas AG Ken Paxton's 2026 Senate campaign — a specific, sizable primary-cycle spend that signals how contested and well-funded the Texas Senate race already is more than a year out.
items.angle: Early, large outside-money commitments like this are a decent leading indicator of which primaries become national proxy fights — worth tracking for how Texas-specific names react if opponents respond in kind.
items.tweetA: $10M from Trump's own Super PAC into Texas Senate attack ads, over a year before the general. That's not normal primary spending — it's a signal the White House already picked its horse in a contested seat.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching the 2026 House map. The money says watch Texas Senate instead — $10M in outside spend this early means someone thinks the primary, not November, is the real fight.

items.title: Trump orders gray wolf protection review, tying ranching relief to beef prices
items.idea: Trump ordered a review of gray wolves' endangered-species protections and directed agencies to let ranchers kill wolves that threaten livestock — reporting explicitly frames the move alongside beef-price pressure, linking a species-protection rollback directly to food-inflation politics.
items.angle: A regulatory rollback justified by consumer prices is a tell that beef/food inflation is politically sensitive enough to touch environmental policy — watch for read-through to cattle futures sentiment and broader ag-deregulation risk.
items.tweetA: Gray wolf protections under review, explicitly framed around beef prices. When food inflation gets bad enough to move endangered-species policy, that's a bigger tell about political tolerance for high grocery prices than any CPI subcomponent.
items.tweetB: Ranchers get a green light to kill wolves threatening livestock. Small policy, but a leading indicator: expect more supply-side deregulation dressed up as inflation relief while beef prices stay sticky.

items.title: Missouri asks SCOTUS to restore a GOP-favored map before the midterms
items.idea: Missouri and Republican state leaders petitioned the Supreme Court to restore a congressional map designed to favor the party ahead of November's midterms — one more state-level redistricting fight reaching the court in a cycle where House control is already tight.
items.angle: Each redistricting fight incrementally shifts the probability distribution on House control — worth tracking as a basket rather than one-off stories for anyone pricing regulatory-agenda risk into 2027.
items.tweetA: Missouri just became the latest state asking the Supreme Court to bless a favorable map before the midterms. This is a pattern now, not an incident — and each ruling moves the real question of who controls regulatory agendas in 2027.
items.tweetB: Nobody trades redistricting rulings directly, but they should be on the same watchlist as Fed dot plots — House control determines whether 2027 is deregulation or reversal, and these map fights decide that a year early.

items.title: US Ambassador calls Israeli settler violence an 'act of terror' — a notable rhetorical break
items.idea: US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, historically one of the administration's strongest pro-settlement voices, called West Bank settler violence an 'act of terror' during a visit focused on affected American residents — a shift in language from a consistently pro-settler official.
items.angle: When your most reliably pro-settlement ambassador uses the word 'terror' about settler violence, that's a bigger signal about shifting policy tolerance than most headline diplomacy — watch for whether it turns into anything concrete.
items.tweetA: Huckabee — as pro-settlement as US ambassadors get — just called West Bank settler violence an 'act of terror.' Words don't move markets, but this particular official using this particular phrase is the kind of small tell that precedes bigger shifts.
items.tweetB: If even Huckabee is done giving settler violence rhetorical cover, watch whether that turns into anything concrete — visa actions, aid conditions, anything. Right now it's just words, but unexpected ones from this messenger.
